languages.truth_bases_notes: One row per `impl <trait> for <type>` and per `trait X: Y`, kind `trait`, because a Rust `impl` is a contract fulfilment and not an ancestry; `impl Point` (inherent) is deliberately absent, because an inherent impl adds members and changes no relationship. `impl fmt::Debug for Shape` names the base as written (`Debug`), not as resolved, because `e3.2` draws the edge and needs the name the reader will look for.
languages.truth_notes: The corpus is a crate root: `lib.rs` declares the module tree, so module paths are derivable. Hand-annotated against the Rust reference, not against any parser. Definitions are what a file *declares*, cfg-gated arms included (a file that declares both arms declares two definitions). Export is the crate's external surface: an item is exported if a file outside this crate could name it in a *default unix build* — which needs the item's own visibility (`pub`, not `pub(crate)`), every module on its path from the crate root being `pub`, and, for an item in a private module, a public re-export somewhere that gives it a public path. That is the reading `e3.7`'s public-API surface needs, and it is the one that makes `pub use` load-bearing: `secret::helper` is public only because `lib.rs` re-exports it. Members are excluded from the export set (top level only). Associated items of an impl for an external type are attributed to the self type's base name (`Vec.measured`), because that is what a graph node for 'method of Vec declared in this file' means.
languages.truth_synthetic_notes: `macros.rs` only. The file declares two `macro_rules!` and invokes both at file scope, so items exist that no token stream contains, and the honest scope is the file — a macro arm is not confined to the item it writes. No other file in this corpus earns the mark: `cfg` arms are text, `#[derive]` is an attribute the extractor can name, and marking a cfg-gated module synthetic would throw away two real definitions to describe a build-time choice.

languages.truth_bases_notes: One row per `class X(Y)`. `NamedTuple` and `TypedDict` are recorded as bases because the corpus classes genuinely declare them, and because the consequence — the members come from the base, not the file — is exactly what the row is for; `resolved` stays absent for them since they live outside the corpus. Python's keyword form `class X(metaclass=M)` would be kind `metaclass`; this corpus has none, and saying so is better than inventing one.
languages.truth_notes: The corpus root is a package, so `from .models import Shape` is a relative import with a determinate target. Export is `__all__` where a module defines one, otherwise every module-level name without a leading underscore — a rule about names, not about declarations, so a re-export (`from .models import Shape` in `__init__.py`) is a definition the file does not have and an export it does not own; those land in the import relation instead. `@dataclass` writes an `__init__`, so a decorated class's generated `__init__` is annotated as a definition: the decorator is documented to do it, and whether a parser knows that is the measured question, not a thing the annotation gets to skip. A module-level binding assigned a `namedtuple(...)` call is a class. Statements inside a function body are not symbols, but imports inside a function body *are* import edges, because Python's lazy imports are load-bearing for the dependency graph.
languages.truth_synthetic_notes: `dynamic.py` and `models.py`. dynamic.py: a module-level `__getattr__` and a `globals()[...]` write put names in the module no file declares (`dynamic_method`), and `Shape.describe = lambda ...`, `Slate.extra = property(...)` write members into classes from the outside (`monkeypatch`); `Box`/`Movie` are a `NamedTuple` and a `TypedDict`, so their members are added by the base (`synthesised_accessors`); `Slate` carries a decorator that replaces the class (`decorated`). models.py: both dataclasses have members `@dataclass` writes (`decorated`, and `synthesised_accessors` because the decorator is known to add `__init__`/`__eq__`/`__repr__`). registry.py is deliberately NOT marked: `@register` writes a dispatch table, not members of a scope, and pretending otherwise would mark half of every Flask application unenumerable — the honest record of it is the `decorated_by:register` modifier, and the category is in `thresholds.json` under `irreducible_blind_spots.python` as `runtime_registration`.

languages.truth_bases_notes: One row per `implements` and per `extends`. `implements Shape` is kind `interface` and `extends Base` is kind `base`, because the two answer different questions — `who fulfils this contract` and `who inherits this state` — and a pane that merges them cannot tell a refactor from a subtype change. This corpus has no `extends` row, which is a gap in the corpus, not a claim about TypeScript.
languages.truth_notes: ES modules. An import of a name re-exported by a barrel resolves to the *origin* file (the barrel is a hop, recorded on the importing file as one edge with `barrel_hop`); a barrel's own export set is empty because it declares nothing. A default export is the exported name `default`, and the local name is an alias. Two `export interface Config` blocks in one file are declaration merging: one symbol, two declaration sites. A module-level binding whose initialiser is a function value is a `fn`, not a `var`. Members are excluded from the export set.
languages.truth_synthetic_notes: index.ts and geo/index.ts are barrels: `export * from './shapes'` means the module's export list is whatever the target exports, which no read of the barrel can enumerate (`wildcard_reexport`). types.d.ts is ambient: an `.d.ts` describes declarations that may be merged by any other `.d.ts` in the program (`ambient_merge`). legacy.ts earns `ambient_merge` for two reasons at once: two `export interface Config` blocks that TypeScript merges into one declaration, and a `declare module 'virtual:thing'` block whose contents a bundler writes into a module that has no file. consumer.ts is NOT marked: it imports names, which is a claim the file can make.

exemption.why: Not a slower grammar — a mis-measured one. A Go import names a package, so the replica (an eleven-file fixture copied 444 times) is a corpus of packages with ~800 files each, and every one of the fixture's imports fans out to all of them: the replica reported 563 resolved edges per file against the fixture's 14. The exemption holds only while the machine-authored repository-shaped corpus in `throughput.repository` — 40 packages of 30 files, one module, every import pointing at a package that exists — clears the files-per-second floor outright and the MiB/s canary scaled to that corpus's own mean file size. Go clears both, which is the evidence that the replica's 0.3 MiB/s is about the replica and not about the grammar.

throughput_check.mean: the replica, measured: files per second per core is the contract because ADR-004's budgets are paid per changed file; MiB/s is reported next to spike s1's parse-only figure to show what resolution adds on top of parsing. A debug build exempts both, because a debug build measures the borrow checker.

languages.truth_bases_notes: One row per embedded field or embedded interface element, because embedding is the only inheritance Go has: `type Options struct { Shape }` gives Options everything Shape has, kind `base`; `type Repo interface { Bucket }` is a contract composed of contracts, kind `interface`. Method sets are not bases — `Shape.Area` is a member of Shape, not a supertype of anything. Go has no `extends` anywhere, so no row here is a `trait`.
languages.truth_notes: Go import resolution is package-granular: an import names a directory, not a file, so a resolved import fans out to every non-test file of the package directory with symbol `*` (the whole package really is visible to the importer). The module path is deduced from the corpus (the extractor is not handed `go.mod`, and will not open a file it was not given), then stripped to find the directory. `*_test.go` files are excluded from the package index — `shape_test.go` declares a *different* package (`shape_test`) in the same directory, which is the dir-to-package mapping trap. The `package` clause is a file's identity, not a definition. Export = first rune is an upper-case letter, which is a name property, not a declaration marker. Two files with `//go:build` constraints both declare `metrics.Init`. Edges are drawn per file of the imported package and every one of them is labelled package-granular: the language's dependency is `main -> shape`, and the file-level rendering is the store's granularity, not the language's (e3.1b, s1 finding 4). The module path is deduced from the corpus (the extractor is not handed `go.mod` and will not open it); an import that fits neither the deduced module nor a corpus-relative path comes back unresolved.
languages.truth_synthetic_notes: `init_linux.go` and `init_other.go` only. Both declare `metrics.Init` and exactly one of them is compiled, which is decided by a `//go:build` line the parser can read and cannot evaluate: a parser does not run the build. So the file's own declaration list is not the package's declaration list, which is a cannot-enumerate state rather than a duplicate definition. No other Go file earns a mark: a second file in the same directory is not a second copy of anything, and `doc.go` declaring nothing is a real answer.

cost.mean: the byte cap divided by the measured rate: the most a cold run can spend on this language, against ADR-004's `cold.graph.ms` small-class budget. This is why a slow grammar is a scan-policy question rather than a feature-gate argument.

scan_budget.mean: s1 finding 7: the feature gates stay and the scan policy is what changes. Ruby is the only language with a cap by default, because it is the only grammar measured an order of magnitude off the pack; files past the cap come back `scan_budget` with their file-level numbers, in the order `extract.ruby.priority` ranked them.

loads.sentence: loading lib/demo.rb pulls in 4 file(s): lib/demo/core/circle.rb, lib/demo/core/shape.rb, lib/demo/report.rb, lib/demo/version.rb

surface.mean: Ruby has no per-symbol access control, so `exports` here is every top-level name the file wrote and nothing more: a surface that prints it under the heading `public symbols` is lying about the language. The question Ruby can answer is the one above - what a require pulls in - and `e3.7` is told to print that instead.

exemption.why: Ruby is the one grammar s1 measured an order of magnitude off the pack (under 1 MiB/s on the replica shape against 11-16 for the others, because the Ruby grammar costs per syntactic construct rather than per byte, and Ruby files are made of constructs). The answer is not a lower accuracy bar and not a dropped grammar; it is a bound that is arithmetic. `extract.ruby.max_bytes_per_run` divided by the measured rate is the most a cold run may spend on Ruby, and the report's `scan_budget.cost` states that number against `graph_budget_ms` (`cold.graph.ms`, the small class). Miss the floor *and* the arithmetic and it is a condition on the run, which is what `verdict_rule` says anyway.

throughput_check.mean: the replica, measured: files per second per core is the contract because ADR-004's budgets are paid per changed file; MiB/s is reported next to spike s1's parse-only figure to show what resolution adds on top of parsing. A debug build exempts both, because a debug build measures the borrow checker.

languages.truth_bases_notes: One row per superclass (`class Circle < Shape`) and per mixin call (`include Mixin`, `prepend`, `extend`), kind `base` for both: Ruby calls a mixin an ancestor, `ancestors` lists it, and there is no separate contract relation to call it. `StandardError` and `Comparable` are annotated even though they are outside the corpus — the base is recorded *as written*, and `resolved: null` is what says the corpus does not declare it.
languages.truth_notes: Ruby's load path is a convention: `require "demo/version"` resolves against a load root that is not stated in the file (the corpus's root is `lib/`), so the corpus is annotated with that root and the extractor must be told it. `require`, `require_relative` and `autoload` are all file-granular: Ruby has no symbol-level import edge at all, so every resolved edge carries symbol `*` and the import relation cannot say *which* name was used. Export is the degenerate case: `module Demo` in five files is one constant, and any public constant or top-level method is nameable from anywhere, so the export set is the public top-level surface and carries almost no information — which is itself the finding. Truth includes the methods `attr_reader`/`attr_accessor`/`define_method`/`alias`/`defdelegate`/`class_eval`/`Struct.new` create, because they exist for every consumer of the class; whether a *parser* can see them is the question this spike asks, not whether Ruby has them. Every Ruby file with an export carries the note `export_surface_is_the_file`: the honest Ruby surface question is which files an entry point loads, and `CorpusStructure::loads` is the query that answers it (e3.1b, s1 finding 3).
languages.truth_synthetic_notes: Three files, two reasons. `shape.rb` and `report.rb` both run `define_method` over a constant array, so the method names exist only at runtime: the scope cannot be enumerated from the file, which is the `dynamic_method` mark and the excuse for the four `define_method_loop` rows. `plugin.rb` reopens `Demo.Core.Shape` with `class_eval` from a file that does not declare it, so *this* file cannot enumerate a class that lives elsewhere — the same state arrived at from the other side, and marked `monkeypatch`. Nothing else is marked: `attr_reader`, `alias`, `Struct.new` and a literal `define_method(:perimeter)` are all in the file, and a parser that cannot see them has a bug, not a blind spot.

corpus.mean: machine-authored, and said out loud: nobody hand-annotates 1 200 Java files. What makes the number worth having is that the generator plants every dependency it expects and nothing else, and fills the type-name pool with the collisions (`Builder`, `Result`, `Config`) that a same-package scan can only get wrong when a name means several files.

without_the_bound_name_rule.mean: the same scoped scan, re-run with the rule that treats a name the file binds itself as a mention switched off. Every added edge is a method type variable spelled like a type another file of the same package declares: the source cannot mean any of them, and a scan that only counts words would clear its recall floor while claiming them. Measured rather than inferred, because a counterfactual computed from the same assumption being tested proves nothing.

same_package.mean: s1 finding 5, measured at repository scale instead of on ten files. Three rules make the scoped column what it is: a reference resolves against the file's own declared package and nowhere else; a single-type import of the same spelling shadows it (JLS 6.5.5); and a name the file itself binds as a type parameter is a mention, not a use. The wide column is the spike's version - every type reference, resolved against any package that declares the name - kept as a measurement so the cost of that reading stays a number. The coarse edge of the shipped scan is stated too: bound names are collected per file, not per scope, so a file that binds `<Result>` and also names the package's `Result` elsewhere loses that one edge, which is a hole rather than a wrong answer.

scan_budget.mean: No per-run cap for this language, on purpose: s1 measured it inside the pack, and a cap that can never bind is decoration. The mechanism is here for the next grammar that costs what Ruby costs.

surface.mean: This language's export rule is a real access rule, so a surface may print its export list as public API.

exemption.why: Same reason and same escape hatch as Go: Java resolves a bare reference against a package, so a 4 000-copy replica resolves every import to ~800 files and reports 719 edges per file. The repository-shaped corpus is the same 1 200-file, 40-package corpus the same-package false-positive rate is published from, so the number is not chosen for the occasion — and it clears the contract floor at ~1 100 files/s.

throughput_check.mean: the replica, measured: files per second per core is the contract because ADR-004's budgets are paid per changed file; MiB/s is reported next to spike s1's parse-only figure to show what resolution adds on top of parsing. A debug build exempts both, because a debug build measures the borrow checker.

languages.truth_bases_notes: One row per `implements` and per `extends`, kind `interface` for a contract and `base` for a superclass. `sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Point, Color` is *not* a supertype row — `permits` lists the subtypes, which is the opposite edge — but it is a real dependency with no import statement to read, so it is annotated on `imports` with the tag `same_package` and is the reason the same-package scan exists at all.
languages.truth_notes: Java names a dependency by package, and the package is a directory: `import com.acme.app.model.Circle` resolves to `com/acme/app/model/Circle.java`, a wildcard import resolves to every file of the directory, and a *same-package* reference needs no statement at all — `sealed interface Shape permits Circle` is a dependency edge with nothing to parse an import out of. Those edges are annotated here (tag `same_package`); whether a parser can find them by scanning type references is the measured question, and the FP risk is that a type-shaped identifier that is not a corpus type produces an edge that is not there. Records generate accessors for their components, and generated members are annotated as definitions, exactly as `@dataclass` members are in Python. Constructors are not symbols; neither are fields, so no Java file has a `const` row. `module-info.java` declares the module and its `exports` list, which is the authority for API surface (`e3.7`) though not for nameability inside this module. Export is the module's external surface: a `public` top-level type in a package that `module-info.java` exports. A package-private type (tag `package_private`) is nameable only inside its own package, and a type in a package the module does not export (`com.acme.app.legacy`) is nameable inside this module but not outside it, so neither is an export — which is why `module-info.java` has to be read, not skipped. Same-package edges are found by scanning unqualified type references and resolving them against the file's own declared package, scoped to exclude anything the file already imports by name (a single-type import shadows a same-package name, JLS 6.5.5) and anything reached through a qualifier. The scope is a config key, `extract.java.same_package_scan`, and the false-positive budget is published in the report (e3.1b, s1 finding 5).
languages.truth_synthetic_notes: `Circle.java` only: `record Circle(String name, double r)` declares two accessors the file does not contain, which is the `synthesised_accessors` mark on the record's own scope and the excuse for the two `record_accessor` rows. Compact constructors are recorded as `constructor` notes, not as scopes: constructors are not symbols by the corpus's rule, so nothing is being hidden from a declaration list that had a right to expect them.

granularity.definitions: one row per named declaration at file top level or inside a type/module container, members included, function-local declarations excluded; a cfg-gated or conditional arm that declares a second copy of a name is the same row, because the graph is a set of names, not a count of tokens
granularity.edge_granularity: one row per (file, unit depended on, symbol). A unit is a file in every language except Go, where an import names a *package*: those edges carry `granularity: package` and the import path, and are drawn once per file of the target package because the record is per file. A pane that prints a package-granular edge as a file-to-file fact is reporting a dependency the language never declared (s1 finding 4).
granularity.exports: one row per top-level symbol nameable from outside the declaring unit, per the language's own access rules
granularity.imports: one row per (file, resolved corpus file, symbol) dependency, with symbol `*` for a dependency whose contents the file does not name
granularity.supertypes: one row per (file, declaring symbol, base as written), kind `base`, `trait`, `interface` or `metaclass`
granularity.synthetic: one row per (file, dotted scope) that cannot be enumerated from the file, with the reason words the extractor uses

thresholds.how_thresholds_are_set: Recall is the bar that matters for a graph, because a missing edge is an invisible dependency and an invisible dependency is the failure ADR-004's whole argument is about. Precision matters more for an export surface, because a wrong `public` is a false promise in a breaking-change report. Each floor is stated as (a) what a reviewer would notice and (b) what a grammar plus a language model can actually deliver, and `hard: true` means 'missing this makes the language unusable for `e3.2`..`e3.7` at file granularity, so it goes to the fallback rather than to a caveat'. The numbers are spike `s1`'s, deliberately: the spike measured what these grammars deliver, and re-measuring its own guess is not how this ticket should move the bar.

irreducible_blind_spots.what: Categories the extractor cannot remove at any effort level, per language, because the information is not in the file. A run that records one of these still passes, but the verdict is `conditions`: the category is stated as a limitation rather than rounded away. Anything the corpus shows that is not listed here is a bug in the extractor, not a property of the language.

irreducible_tags.what: The annotation tags whose *definition rows* are removed from the scored set, because the declaration is not textually in the file at all: a `macro_rules!` arm, a `@dataclass`-written `__init__`, a monkeypatched method, a webpack virtual module. This is not leniency wearing a hat — the alternative is scoring the extractor against rows no file-granularity parser can produce, which teaches it to guess. What the extractor owes instead is the honest state, and `mechanisms.synthetic_eligible` is where that debt is collected: the scope the row lives in must come back marked.

mechanisms.never_lost: Every input file returns a record. A file with no structure returns a reason and its file-level measurement. Losing a file is the failure mode that turns a wrong number into an invisible one.
mechanisms.resolution: Resolution is a bounded iteration, and the bound is a config key, and the report says how many passes were used and whether the file converged. Non-convergence is a bug to fix, not a caveat; `--max-passes 1` exists so the bound can be shown to bite rather than asserted.
mechanisms.synthetic_eligible: Every scope the corpus marks must come back marked. A marked scope must never produce a 'declares nothing' assertion: the surface may say 'may have shrunk, not shrunk', and nothing stronger. Missing a scope is a fail, not a condition, because an unmarked dynamic scope is a confidently wrong answer about code that changed.
mechanisms.what: The four checks in the report's `mechanisms` block, and what each one costs when it fails. These are not extra accuracy metrics — they are the four ways a clean set score can still describe a useless extractor, which is the argument spike `s1` spent its planning budget making.
mechanisms.wildcard_edges: Every `*` import in the corpus must arrive as its own edge kind, and `dependents_of` must answer 'who depends on X' by naming the wildcard files as *unknown-content dependents*. Reporting a star import as a resolved named edge, or answering 'nobody', is a fail: both are the same lie told twice.

definitions.mean: A definition is one named declaration at file top level or inside a type/module container, members included, function-local declarations excluded. Missing 5 % of them means 5 % of the code has no node in the graph, and a file with no node cannot be reviewed.

exports.mean: One row per top-level symbol nameable from outside the declaring unit, per the language's own access rules — Rust's re-export rule, Python's `__all__`-or-underscore rule, TypeScript's `export`-plus-barrel rule. Precision is the higher bar here: a false `public` is a wrong breaking-change report, which is worse than a missing one.

imports.mean: One row per (file, resolved corpus file, symbol) dependency, wildcard rows included with symbol `*`. Ten percent is the price of dynamic module systems — a Python `importlib.import_module` and a TypeScript namespace import are genuinely unresolvable at file granularity.

supertypes.mean: One row per declared base, implemented trait or implemented interface. Recall is the higher bar: `who implements Shape?` is the question the architecture pane draws, and a missing `impl` is a hole in the shape of the system.

same_package.mean: Of the edges the scan claims, at most 2 % may be edges the corpus does not contain, and at least 95 % of the dependencies the corpus plants must be found. Both are re-measured from the report by `tests/test_structure_tail_contract.py`, and `--check` refuses a report whose numbers moved, so the budget is arithmetic in CI rather than a paragraph in a design document. The corpus is machine-authored (see `java_corpus.rs` and the report's `same_package.corpus.mean`), which is the only honest way to get 1 200 Java files with a known dependency set; what makes the number worth having is that the generator plants the shadowing imports, the package-qualified heads and the bound type variables that a naive same-package scan gets wrong, and counts the baits so the counterfactual rate is checkable.
same_package.what: The budget for Java same-package resolution, which is the one place in the extractor where false-positive risk is a feature rather than an accident. Spike `s1` found 14 of 14 same-package edges with zero false positives on a ten-file corpus; `e0.12` turned that into `e3.1b`'s third acceptance criterion — re-measure on at least 1 000 files, publish the rate, state the budget — and made `e3.2` wait for it before drawing same-package edges at all.

throughput.comment: Parse-plus-extract throughput per core, release profile, measured on a deterministic 4 000-file replica of the corpus because 9 fixture files measure process startup. ADR-004's `cold.graph.ms` and `warm.graph.marginal.ms` are paid per changed file, so files-per-second-per-core is the contract and 1 000 files/s clears a 5 000-file warm pass by three orders of magnitude. The MiB/s figure is a canary, stated second because source files are small and uneven: spike `s1` measured 5 MiB/s parse-only, and this number is parse *plus* resolution, whose cost grows with the corpus rather than the file. Both floors are enforced in a release build and exempt in a debug build, which measures bounds checks rather than the extractor.

go.why: Not a slower grammar — a mis-measured one. A Go import names a package, so the replica (an eleven-file fixture copied 444 times) is a corpus of packages with ~800 files each, and every one of the fixture's imports fans out to all of them: the replica reported 563 resolved edges per file against the fixture's 14. The exemption holds only while the machine-authored repository-shaped corpus in `throughput.repository` — 40 packages of 30 files, one module, every import pointing at a package that exists — clears the files-per-second floor outright and the MiB/s canary scaled to that corpus's own mean file size. Go clears both, which is the evidence that the replica's 0.3 MiB/s is about the replica and not about the grammar.

java.why: Same reason and same escape hatch as Go: Java resolves a bare reference against a package, so a 4 000-copy replica resolves every import to ~800 files and reports 719 edges per file. The repository-shaped corpus is the same 1 200-file, 40-package corpus the same-package false-positive rate is published from, so the number is not chosen for the occasion — and it clears the contract floor at ~1 100 files/s.

ruby.why: Ruby is the one grammar s1 measured an order of magnitude off the pack (under 1 MiB/s on the replica shape against 11-16 for the others, because the Ruby grammar costs per syntactic construct rather than per byte, and Ruby files are made of constructs). The answer is not a lower accuracy bar and not a dropped grammar; it is a bound that is arithmetic. `extract.ruby.max_bytes_per_run` divided by the measured rate is the most a cold run may spend on Ruby, and the report's `scan_budget.cost` states that number against `graph_budget_ms` (`cold.graph.ms`, the small class). Miss the floor *and* the arithmetic and it is a condition on the run, which is what `verdict_rule` says anyway.

thresholds.verdict_rule: pass: every relation at or above its floor, and no mechanism missed, and the throughput floor met in a release build. conditions: every `hard` floor met, but a soft floor missed, a row missed or found that the floors tolerate, or an irreducible blind spot recorded. fail: a `hard` floor missed, or any mechanism check missed — a mechanism is not a quality bar, it is the definition of what the output is allowed to claim.
thresholds.what: The acceptance bar for `e3.1` (`reco-zoz`) and its tail `e3.1b` (`reco-dlp.1`): the structural extractor for six languages, plus the mechanisms spike `s1` handed over as non-negotiables and the three scan-policy knobs `e0.12` attached to the tail. A language that misses a `hard` floor is not cut from the plan — it is stated as what this build does not do, in the report and in `docs/concepts/structure-extraction.md`, and the language's files come back with a reason instead of a silently thin graph.
